rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds and identify crowded retention regions. A moderate gradient duration and midpoint temperature leave room to optimize selectivity, resolution, and run time.

All peaks are comfortably resolved, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty. Keeping temperature and endpoints fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the crowded middle peaks.
The shorter gradient eliminates the time penalty but compresses a middle cluster. Raising temperature tests whether altered selectivity can separate that cluster while retaining the fast elution.

The temperature shift suggests an elution-order crossover within the middle cluster. A hotter, steeper gradient tests the other side of that crossover for improved separation while preserving zero time penalty.

Test the low-temperature end to explore a different selectivity regime for the middle cluster. The 10-minute gradient should retain a small or zero time penalty while revealing whether cooling resolves the critical pairs.

Combine high-temperature selectivity with a shallower gradient to separate the close pair seen at 60 C. The last peak should still elute before approximately 8 minutes, preserving the zero time penalty.
The best run has only one under-resolved pair, while further heating worsens it. Raise the starting organic fraction to test a different selectivity balance at 55 C without adding a time penalty.

Cooling slightly from the best run should improve the close fourth–fifth peak separation, while a modestly shallower gradient may preserve resolution elsewhere in the middle cluster. The projected last-peak time remains near the zero-penalty region.
At the 12-minute gradient, 50 C and 60 C favor different critical pairs; 55 C should balance their separations. The last peak is expected before 8 minutes, retaining zero time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already attained; this run tests an alternative with potentially more separation margin. A shallower gradient may offset the selectivity shift from higher starting organic while keeping the last peak near the zero-penalty window.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness relative to injection 9 to test whether the critical-pair resolution margin improves. The last peak is projected near 8 minutes, potentially preserving the maximum CRF with zero time penalty.

A slightly shallower gradient than injection 10 should raise its marginal resolution of 1.47 above 1.5 while retaining separation of the other critical pair. This tests another maximum-score method, although the predicted last-peak time is close to the time-penalty boundary.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction combined with a shallower gradient preserves full resolution and zero time penalty. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method; this run explores an alternative selectivity balance.

This preserves injection 9's starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope of 0.075 per minute. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end, it should retain the maximum CRF while using a lower final organic fraction.

Preserve the maximum-score gradient slope while lowering the endpoint again. The gradient reaches its final composition at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after all peaks previously eluted, so the chromatogram should remain unchanged.

This gradient slope lies between injections 10 and 12, targeting resolution above 1.5 for both critical pairs with the last peak below 8 minutes. It may match the maximum CRF with slightly more resolution margin than injection 9.

Preserve injection 12's gradient slope and starting composition with a lower endpoint. Because its last peak eluted before the new gradient ends at the outlet, this should reproduce its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of approximately 1.58.

Keep the proven gradient slope through elution of the first nine peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the isolated last peak still elutes before 8 minutes, preserving maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Injection 18 shows that zero time penalty extends beyond 8 minutes. A shallower gradient than injection 13 may resolve its critical pair while retaining the stronger separation of the other middle pair, potentially matching maximum CRF with greater resolution margin.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly from injection 19 to bring its critical resolution above 1.5 while preserving the other pair's margin. The last peak is projected near 9 minutes, testing whether this alternative can also achieve maximum CRF.

Use a slightly shallower gradient than injection 12 to increase the fourth–fifth peak separation while checking that the other critical pair remains resolved. The projected last-peak time is within the demonstrated zero-penalty range, so this should provide another maximum-score option.

Slightly lower the endpoint from injection 21 to probe the shallower-gradient boundary of the maximum-score region. The observed trends suggest both critical pairs should remain above 1.5 and the last peak should elute within the demonstrated zero-penalty window.
This slope falls between injections 21 and 22, both of which achieved maximum CRF. It should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a gradient slope between injections 21 and 23, where both critical pairs remained resolved with zero time penalty. This should match the maximum CRF while further lowering the final organic fraction.

This slightly shallower gradient should retain full resolution, with the last peak projected within the demonstrated zero-time-penalty range. It tests a lower-endpoint alternative; injection 9 has already achieved the highest possible CRF of 1.000.
